When the Law of the Streets confronted the Men in Uniform!
items.description: By Jimmy Aglah Once upon a time in the Republic of Uncommon Sense, the rule of law went on a brief holiday, leaving behind two gentlemen to look after the Republic. One was a minister of state, armed with the authority of government and the confidence of an elected representative. The other was a military officer, armed with the authority of the Ghana Armed Forces and, presumably, the confidence that comes with commanding men who carry rifles. Unfortunately, nobody appeared to have informed either gentleman where his authority ended and the other’s began. The resulting encounter was a magnificent demonstration of what happens when two institutions of the Republic meet at a roadside without first agreeing on which chapter of the Constitution they are operating under. At the centre of this national drama was Samuel Nartey George, Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, who had temporarily exchanged the complicated business of digital transformation for the more immediate challenge of transforming military behaviour in his Ningo-Prampram constituency. The minister was furious. And judging by the allegations he made, he had reasons to be. Soldiers had allegedly seized tipper trucks, brutalised residents and conducted themselves in a manner that suggested the difference between a military operation and a highway robbery was becoming increasingly difficult to explain to the ordinary taxpayer. There were even allegations that police officers had been threatened with weapons. If true, this would represent a remarkable development in our national security architecture. The police, whose constitutional responsibility includes maintaining law and order, would apparently require protection from soldiers who had arrived to maintain another variety of law and order. In the Republic of Uncommon Sense, such arrangements are not entirely unusual. We have perfected the art of creating institutions to supervise institutions, only to discover that the supervisors occasionally need supervision themselves. But Sam George was not prepared to supervise this particular situation from the comfort of an air-conditioned office. He confronted the military officer, Lieutenant Albert Goh, and proceeded to deliver what might generously be described as an unscheduled lecture in military accountability, constitutional responsibility and the consequences of irritating an elected representative. At one point, the minister reportedly described the soldiers’ conduct in terms associated with armed robbery and demanded the officer’s dismissal. Then came the statement that elevated an otherwise local confrontation into a national philosophical debate. The minister invoked the law of the streets. Now, this was a fascinating constitutional innovation. For decades, Ghanaian lawyers have wasted precious time studying the 1992 Constitution, Acts of Parliament, legislative instruments and judicial precedents. Law students have spent sleepless nights memorising provisions that ordinary citizens struggle to understand. Yet here was a senior government official introducing an entirely new branch of jurisprudence in broad daylight. The Law of the Streets! Nobody knew when Parliament had passed it, whether the President had assented to it or whether copies were available at the Assembly Press. But from the confidence with which it was invoked, one suspected it had been in force for some time, awaiting a suitable military officer on whom to test its provisions. The beauty of this new law was its simplicity. Unlike conventional legislation, it required no parliamentary debate, no committee hearings and no publication in the Gazette. Its enforcement mechanism appeared to depend entirely on how angry the person invoking it had become. One could almost imagine the bewilderment of the military officer. He had probably received instructions from his superiors before embarking on the operation. Whether those instructions authorised everything allegedly done was another matter requiring investigation. But nowhere in his military training, one suspects, had he encountered a minister threatening consequences under a legal framework administered by the streets. And yet the minister’s anger raised a serious question that the Republic could not conveniently dismiss. What exactly were armed soldiers doing in an operation involving tipper trucks and sand-winning activities? Under whose authority were the vehicles allegedly seized? What offences had their owners committed? And if police officers were indeed threatened, had the Republic reached the extraordinary stage where one security institution could intimidate another while both claimed to be enforcing the law? These were not small questions. A soldier’s uniform is not a certificate of exemption from the Constitution. Neither is a rifle an alternative to a court order. If the allegations against the soldiers are established, those responsible must face the appropriate consequences. But there was another little difficulty. A minister’s appointment letter is equally not a licence to establish a parallel judicial system at the roadside. The Republic cannot complain that soldiers have exceeded their authority and then applaud a minister for appearing to exceed his own. Otherwise, we shall eventually arrive at the absurd situation where every public official carries a personal interpretation of the law, to be activated whenever his blood pressure rises. The police will enforce the criminal law. Soldiers will enforce military instructions. Ministers will enforce the law of the streets. And ordinary citizens, caught between these competing jurisdictions, will be left wondering which authority to obey before somebody decides they are obstructing justice. Fortunately, the controversy eventually travelled from the roadside to the conference room. Sam George met the Defence Minister and the military high command, where the temperature of the discussion appears to have dropped considerably. The minister clarified that his remarks were not intended as an attack on the Ghana Armed Forces as an institution, while the military leadership reportedly undertook to investigate the incident. This was reassuring. Apparently, the Republic still possessed functioning institutions capable of resolving disputes without consulting the law of the streets. But the meeting also exposed one of our enduring national habits. We are very enthusiastic about institutional authority when exercising it and remarkably sensitive about institutional respect when somebody else challenges us. The military deserves respect, certainly. Its officers and men perform difficult duties in the service of the Republic. But respect cannot become a protective umbrella under which alleged misconduct is sheltered from scrutiny. Equally, ministers deserve respect for the offices they occupy. But public office demands restraint precisely when anger seems most justified. The higher one climbs the ladder of authority, the less freedom one should have to turn personal indignation into public threats. A Ghanaian proverb reminds us that when two elephants fight, it is the grass that suffers. In this particular contest, however, the grass had already allegedly lost its tipper trucks before the elephants began arguing about constitutional authority. And that is the tragedy beneath the comedy. Somewhere in Ningo-Prampram are ordinary citizens whose livelihoods may have been disrupted. They are not interested in whether a minister can outshout a lieutenant or whether a lieutenant can outstare a minister. They want to know whether their rights were violated, whether their property was lawfully handled and whether anybody will be held accountable. Those questions deserve answers, not merely a reconciliation photograph and a promise to investigate. The Republic must therefore resist the temptation to turn this episode into another contest of personalities. The central issue is not whether Sam George is brave or abrasive, or whether the military officer was sufficiently respectful to a minister. It is whether the law applies equally to the man carrying the rifle, the man carrying the ministerial title and the ordinary citizen carrying the burden of their decisions. For if the allegations against the soldiers are true, the Republic has a military accountability problem. And if ministers believe they can remedy such problems by invoking the law of the streets, we have acquired an additional constitutional problem. One cannot extinguish a fire by pouring petrol on it and then demand applause for displaying concern about fire safety. Perhaps the Attorney-General should now commission a comprehensive review of this newly discovered Law of the Streets, just to establish its relationship with the 1992 Constitution. Until then, the citizens of the Republic of Uncommon Sense would be well advised to travel with three essential documents: their national identity card, their driver’s licence and a certified copy of whichever law happens to be in force on the particular street they are using. Because in a country where soldiers allegedly seize trucks, ministers threaten street justice and everybody claims to be defending the rule of law, the ordinary citizen faces one increasingly difficult question: If those entrusted with enforcing the law cannot agree on what the law is, who exactly is supposed to obey it?

items.title: Labé : armé d’un couteau, un jeune tente d’agresser un imam de Tata 2 en pleine prière
items.description: Une scène de panique s’est produite ce vendredi 6 novembre 2026 dans la mosquée de Yérandé, située au quartier Tata 2, dans la commune urbaine de Labé. En pleine prière du vendredi, un jeune homme muni d’un couteau aurait tenté de s’en prendre au deuxième imam de la mosquée, alors que celui-ci dirigeait l’office religieux. Selon les informations recueillies, les faits se sont déroulés aux environs de 13 h 40. Le jeune homme, présenté comme un élève d’une école coranique située à proximité, aurait fait irruption dans la mosquée avant de se diriger vers le mihrab, où se trouvait l’imam. La réaction rapide des muezzins présents aux côtés de l’imam a permis d’éviter le pire. L’un d’eux aurait réussi à intercepter et à maîtriser le jeune homme, avec le concours de certains responsables du quartier. La prière a ensuite pu se poursuivre normalement. Joint au téléphone, Mamadou Mouctar Diallo, adjoint au président du conseil de quartier de Tata 2, a confirmé les faits et apporté des précisions sur les circonstances de l’incident. « Par la grâce de Dieu, l’acte n’est pas allé à son terme. C’est aux environs de 13 h 40, au moment de la prière, qu’un jeune inscrit dans une école coranique tout près de chez nous est venu armé d’un couteau. Il a foncé vers le mihrab. Heureusement, le deuxième muezzin l’a bloqué et l’a ceinturé avec force », a-t-il expliqué. Notre interlocuteur affirme également que le jeune homme aurait auparavant proféré des menaces à l’encontre de l’imam. Selon son témoignage, le mis en cause aurait exprimé son intention de l’éliminer, estimant que c’était à lui de lui succéder. Il précise que le cheikh du jeune aurait auparavant pris des engagements pour assurer sa surveillance, mais que ces dispositions n’auraient pas été respectées. Alertés, les services de sécurité, notamment la gendarmerie, se sont rendus sur les lieux. À l’issue des échanges entre les responsables du quartier et le cheikh du jeune, ce dernier aurait pris l’engagement de conduire son élève à Conakry afin qu’il bénéficie d’une prise en charge médicale. Selon les informations recueillies, le jeune mis en cause aurait finalement été conduit vers la capitale pour une évaluation de son état de santé mentale. Cet incident suscite de nombreuses réactions au sein de la population de Labé. Aucune communication officielle n’a toutefois été faite concernant d’éventuelles poursuites judiciaires ou les conclusions de la prise en charge médicale. Alpha Moussa Dieng, correspondant régional à Labé L’article Labé : armé d’un couteau, un jeune tente d’agresser un imam de Tata 2 en pleine prière est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Traffitech rollout: What Ghana can learn from countries that warn motorists about speed cameras
items.description: By Jimmy Aglah The rollout of Ghana’s automated traffic enforcement system, Traffitech, has brought into sharp focus an important aspect of road safety management: the responsibility of authorities to provide motorists with adequate road signs before enforcing traffic regulations. As concerns grow over inadequate speed-limit signs and the absence of advance warnings about enforcement cameras, experiences from developed jurisdictions suggest that Ghana could benefit from a more comprehensive approach that combines technology, clear road signage, public education and effective enforcement. In countries such as the United Kingdom, France and Australia, warning signs are widely used to alert motorists to speed cameras, although the legal requirements and enforcement policies differ. The underlying policy question is whether motorists should be encouraged to comply with speed limits before reaching enforcement points or whether authorities should rely principally on detecting and penalising violations after they occur. Ghana’s road infrastructure comes under scrutiny Traffitech, which commenced operation on November 1, 2026, uses cameras and other electronic devices to detect traffic violations, including speeding and running red lights. The system is intended to improve compliance with road traffic regulations and reduce crashes, injuries and fatalities. However, its introduction has exposed concerns about the adequacy of the country’s road infrastructure, particularly the visibility and availability of speed-limit signs. On Wednesday, November 4, the Director-General of the National Road Safety Authority (NRSA), Abraham Amaliba, acknowledged these concerns during an interview on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show. He announced that Traffitech cameras would initially operate only on roads where speed limits were clearly displayed. Mr Amaliba argued that it would be unfair to penalise motorists for failures attributable to the authorities responsible for providing road infrastructure. He cited Boundary Road towards Mahama Road in Accra, where a speed limit of 50 kilometres per hour is displayed, as an example of a road where automated enforcement could operate. The NRSA Director-General also acknowledged concerns about the absence of advance camera warning signs and indicated that steps would be considered to give motorists adequate notice. He explained that the Department of Urban Roads, Department of Feeder Roads and Ghana Highway Authority would have responsibility for providing the necessary signs. His comments followed a meeting on November 3 involving government officials, the police and transport operators to address concerns surrounding the implementation of Traffitech. Police guidance raises a separate question The Ghana Police Service’s official Traffitech guidance provides important clarification on the legal position. According to the police, some roads and intersections have warning signs announcing enforcement cameras, while others do not. The guidance states that there is no general legal obligation to announce traffic enforcement operations and that the absence of a camera warning sign does not invalidate a traffic offence. It further explains that licensed drivers are expected to know the statutory speed limits prescribed under the Road Traffic Regulations, 2026 (L.I. 2519), whether or not a speed-limit sign is displayed. The police identify general speed limits including 30 kilometres per hour in specified areas of predominant human activity, 50 kilometres per hour in urban or built-up areas, 90 kilometres per hour on highways and 100 kilometres per hour on motorways. This introduces an important distinction between the legal obligations of motorists and the operational policy announced by the NRSA. While motorists remain legally responsible for complying with applicable speed limits, the NRSA has indicated that automated enforcement will initially be restricted to roads with adequate speed-limit signs. There is also a distinction between speed-limit signs and camera warning signs. The former communicate the maximum permissible speed, while the latter alert motorists to the presence of automated enforcement equipment. Both can contribute to safer driving, but they perform different functions. NRSA orders urgent improvements to road signs The concerns have prompted official action. In a letter dated November 3, 2026, the NRSA directed the Ghana Highway Authority and Department of Urban Roads to urgently address deficiencies in road infrastructure, including missing signs, faded road markings, faulty traffic lights and inadequate street lighting. The Authority warned that these deficiencies could undermine the effectiveness of Traffitech and compromise road safety. The agencies were also asked to provide timelines for completing the necessary improvements. The directive underscores the importance of ensuring that physical road infrastructure keeps pace with the deployment of digital enforcement technology. United Kingdom: Warning signs are common but not compulsory In the United Kingdom, speed camera warning signs are a familiar feature of the road network. The signs typically display a camera symbol to alert motorists to the possibility of automated speed enforcement. However, British police guidance makes clear that there is no general legal requirement for fixed or mobile speed cameras to be accompanied by warning signs. Their use is instead governed by operational policies and best-practice guidance. This means that motorists can be prosecuted for speeding even where no advance camera warning has been provided. Nevertheless, the widespread use of camera warning signs demonstrates that authorities can combine enforcement with measures intended to encourage drivers to moderate their speed. France: Fixed speed cameras are announced France operates an extensive automated speed enforcement system in which fixed speed cameras are generally announced through roadside warning signs. These signs alert drivers to the presence of enforcement equipment and encourage them to observe the applicable speed limits. However, the French system distinguishes between fixed and mobile enforcement. Mobile speed cameras may operate without advance warning, while red-light enforcement cameras are not subject to the same general warning arrangements. The French approach illustrates how advance warnings can form part of a broader traffic enforcement strategy without eliminating the use of less visible enforcement methods. Australia: A policy lesson from New South Wales One of the clearest examples of the role of advance camera warnings comes from New South Wales, Australia. The state operates an extensive automated speed enforcement programme, with fixed cameras installed at locations selected on the basis of road safety considerations, including crash histories and vehicle speeds. According to the New South Wales Government, every regular fixed speed camera is accompanied by highly visible advance warning signs. Three signs are installed on the approach to a regular fixed camera, informing motorists that a camera operates ahead, reminding them of the applicable speed limit and warning of the consequences of speeding. Importantly, the government acknowledges that these advisory signs are not legally mandatory. Their installation is a deliberate transport policy intended to alert motorists before they reach enforcement points. The authorities also publish information about fixed camera locations, including the reasons for their installation. The state’s experience with mobile speed cameras is particularly instructive. In 2020, the New South Wales Government removed advance warning signs from mobile camera operations as part of efforts to strengthen enforcement. The decision attracted public criticism amid a substantial increase in speeding infringements. The government subsequently reversed the policy and restored advance warning signs. The controversy highlighted competing approaches to traffic enforcement: using cameras to detect speeding wherever it occurs, and using visible warnings to encourage motorists to slow down before reaching enforcement locations. Today, New South Wales uses warning signs for mobile speed camera operations as well as fixed installations. Australia does not, however, have a uniform national policy. In Victoria, mobile speed cameras may operate without advance warning signs. The different approaches demonstrate that the use of warning signs is ultimately a policy choice, even in jurisdictions with sophisticated road safety systems. Should Ghana publish camera locations? Another lesson from international practice concerns transparency. In New South Wales, authorities publish the locations of fixed speed cameras and explain the road safety considerations behind their installation. Such disclosures help motorists understand where enforcement is taking place and why particular roads have been selected. For Ghana, publishing an accessible list or map of fixed Traffitech camera locations, together with the applicable speed limits, could improve public awareness and confidence. This would not necessarily require the disclosure of mobile enforcement locations, which may change according to operational needs. The objective would be to make fixed enforcement more transparent while preserving the ability of authorities to address dangerous driving across the wider road network. Measuring success beyond the number of fines The ultimate test of Traffitech will be whether it contributes to safer roads. The number of speeding violations detected and fines imposed may provide useful enforcement data, but these figures alone cannot establish whether the system is achieving its road safety objectives. A more comprehensive assessment would examine changes in vehicle speeds, compliance levels, road crashes, injuries and fatalities. It would also consider whether enforcement locations have adequate signs, road markings and other safety infrastructure. International experience suggests that advance warnings and automated enforcement need not be competing approaches. Both can contribute to a system designed to discourage dangerous driving and encourage compliance. The challenge for Ghana is to ensure that the technology is supported by clear regulations, adequate infrastructure and transparent implementation. The NRSA’s decision to restrict initial enforcement to roads with displayed speed limits, together with its directive for urgent improvements to road infrastructure, represents an acknowledgement of these concerns. Its indication that advance camera warnings will be considered also opens the door to a broader discussion about the role of signage in automated traffic enforcement. Ultimately, the success of Traffitech should not be judged solely by the number of motorists caught violating traffic regulations. It should be measured by the extent to which motorists change their behaviour, observe speed limits and contribute to a reduction in road crashes. For Ghana, the most important question is not simply how many speeding motorists Traffitech can catch, but how many it can persuade to slow down before an accident occurs. items.title: Pourparlers tripartites à Abou Dhabi : les délégations se précisent, Kiev se lance dans le sabotage
items.description: a l'approche des negociations tripartites entre la Russie, les etats-Unis et l'Ukraine, prevues les 10 et 11 novembre a Abou Dhabi, le porte-parole du Kremlin, Dmitri Peskov, a annonce la composition de la delegation russe. Conduite par le conseiller presidentiel Vladimir Medinsky, celle-ci comprendra les vice-ministres des Affaires etrangeres Sergueï Riabkov et Mikhaïl Galouzine, ainsi que deux representants de l'etat-major general des forces armees russes : Igor Kostioukov, chef du service de renseignement militaire, et son adjoint, Iouri Zhigarlovskiï. Du cote ukrainien, les negociations seront menees par le chef des services de renseignement exterieur ukrainiens, Roustem Oumerov. Selon les medias ukrainiens, le chef du cabinet de Zelensky, Kirill Boudanov, se joindra egalement a la delegation. Washington sera represente par Steve Witkoff, envoye special du president americain Donald Trump, et Jared Kushner, son gendre et negociateur sur l'Ukraine. a l'approche d'un nouveau cycle de negociations, Zelensky seme la zizanie Plus les negociations de paix tripartites approchent, plus Volodymyr Zelensky exprime ses craintes. Le chef du regime de Kiev a notamment critique l'initiative de Jared Kushner visant a associer la Russie aux discussions sur la nouvelle architecture de securite europeenne, la qualifiant de « dangereuse » avant tout pour l'UE. Fin octobre, la porte-parole du ministere russe des Affaires etrangeres, Maria Zakharova, avait denonce les tentatives de Zelensky visant a empecher la reprise des negociations entre Moscou et Washington sur le reglement du conflit. Selon elle, le chef du regime de Kiev avance publiquement des conditions « manifestement inacceptables » et autorise de nouvelles attaques terroristes contre des civils russes. La diplomate russe a souligne que Zelensky tentait ainsi de prolonger le conflit afin de conserver son pouvoir personnel. Washington n'exclut pas l'implication de l'Europe en cas de succes a Abou Dhabi, Moscou remet en question ses capacites de mediation L'Europe exige avec vehemence d'etre presente aux negociations. Cette exigence a ete formulee par Kaja Kallas, chef de la diplomatie europeenne, qui a parallelement rejete categoriquement le projet americain visant a restructurer l'architecture de la defense europeenne avec la participation de la Russie. Jared Kushner a, pour sa part, indique qu'en cas de succes lors des pourparlers d'Abou Dhabi, les pays europeens pourraient etre associes a une phase ulterieure des negociations. La Russie, quant a elle, doute du bien-fonde d'une telle participation. Selon Dmitri Peskov, si l'Europe doit etre presente autour de la table pour le reglement du conflit ukrainien, cela n'est pas possible compte tenu de son approche actuelle. D'apres lui, seuls deux dirigeants europeens — le president finlandais Alexander Stubb et le Premier ministre norvegien Jonas Gahr Store — ont a ce jour choisi de dialoguer avec Moscou a titre national, tandis que la majorite des autres pays europeens ne parlent encore que d'infliger une defaite strategique a la Russie. Le ministre russe des Affaires etrangeres, Sergueï Lavrov, a egalement mis en doute la capacite des Europeens a jouer un role constructif dans les negociations. Il a souligne que l'Europe avait manque l'occasion de jouer un role de mediateur, rappelant l'echec des accords conclus en 2014 entre l'ancien president ukrainien et l'opposition, ainsi que celui des accords de Minsk. Paris et Berlin s'etaient portes garants de ces textes, mais n'avaient finalement pas reussi a en assurer la mise en œuvre.

items.title: Kalu urges Igbo leaders to unite, engage in Nigerian politics
items.description: Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, Benjamin Kalu, has urged Igbo elders, leaders and stakeholders to unite and take a more active role in Nigeria’s politics, warning that disunity and political apathy have weakened the South-East’s influence in national affairs. The call was contained in a statement issued on Saturday by his Chief Press Secretary, Levinus Nwabughiogu. Kalu also called for a change of mindset among Igbo people, particularly those who have traditionally focused on developing their communities while keeping away from national politics. He made the call on Friday at the South-East Stakeholders’ Convergence, also known as the South-East Elders and Stakeholders Meeting, held at the Imo State Government House, Owerri. The meeting, convened to discuss unity, peace and development in Igbo land, was chaired by a former Military Governor of Imo State and Minister of Foreign Affairs, Senator Ike Nwachukwu. Kalu, who represents Bende Federal Constituency of Abia State, said unity was essential to the political relevance and development of the South-East, stressing that the region could achieve more if its leaders and people worked towards common goals. “Unity is strength. We will achieve more when we are united. The need for unity cannot be overemphasised. Peace leads to the development of communities,” he said. Commending the elders and stakeholders for attending the meeting despite their individual engagements, the Deputy Speaker described their gathering as an expression of patriotism and commitment to the progress of Igbo land. He said their example would encourage younger generations to sustain the quest for unity and development, likening leadership to a relay race in which older generations hand over the baton to their successors. Kalu, however, warned that the Igbo people risked losing their heritage and political direction if they continued to operate in isolation. On the region’s political influence, he said the numerical strength of the Igbo was not adequately reflected in the political fortunes of the five South-East states, partly because many people from the region lived in other parts of the country. He argued that a common political agenda would enable the Igbo to consolidate their strength and make their voices more influential in national decision-making. “The number of votes of Ndi Igbo is not what we are getting across the five states because we are scattered around the country. If we take a position now and say, Igbo, this is our agenda, this is what we want to do, I can assure you, the whole of Nigeria will feel our impact,” he said. The Deputy Speaker also urged the people to abandon what he described as the post-civil war mindset of avoiding national politics and concentrating solely on developing their communities. According to him, the approach has not yielded the desired political results, making it necessary for the region to become more actively involved in Nigeria’s governance. “After the war, we had believed we will work it out on our own and develop our place. We say we are not interested in politics. It is not our business. We have tried to develop on our own. It is about time we changed that mindset. “The politics and governance of Nigeria should be our concern. We should get involved and play an active role because if we are not in the room, we can’t be part of the decision. We need to be part of the decision-making process,” he said. Kalu called on Igbo leaders to agree on a common position and pursue it collectively, insisting that the region would command greater respect and achieve better results through political cooperation. The meeting was attended by Imo State Governor Hope Uzodimma, traditional rulers, representatives of religious organisations, women and youth groups from the five South-East states, as well as prominent figures from politics, business and academia. Among those present were former Senate President and Secretary to the Government of the Federation, Senator Anyim Pius Anyim; former Vice-Chancellor of the Federal University of Technology, Owerri, Prof. Nnenna Oti; former Chairman of the Police Service Commission, Chief Simeon Okeke; and former President-General of Ohanaeze Ndigbo, Nze Ozichukwu Chukwu. Others included Chief Tony Chukwu, Ambassador Greg Mbadiwe, Prof. Osita Ogbu, Mazi Sam Ohuabunwa and Ambassador Okey Emuche. The post Kalu urges Igbo leaders to unite, engage in Nigerian politics appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Controlled delivery allows drug suspects to remain unaware of investigations – NACOC
items.description: The Deputy Director of the Narcotics Control Commission (NACOC), Alexander Barimah Twum, has explained that suspected drug couriers are deliberately kept unaware during controlled-delivery operations to enable investigators to identify other members of trafficking networks and uncover weaknesses in the country’s enforcement systems. He said the strategy allows law enforcement agencies to monitor suspected drug shipments without alerting the individuals transporting them, thereby creating an opportunity to trace those behind the trafficking activities. Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, Mr Twum said one of the key objectives of controlled delivery was to identify the people orchestrating drug trafficking operations rather than focus solely on the individuals physically carrying the substances. He explained that suspects were not informed when intelligence about their activities had been shared with law enforcement agencies, as maintaining secrecy was essential to the success of the operation. “When we are doing controlled delivery on you, you, the individual, are kept in the dark and you don’t know what is happening,” he said. Mr Twum added that the operation also enabled NACOC to examine loopholes and lapses within its own systems that criminal networks could exploit to facilitate drug trafficking. He said investigators were therefore pursuing two objectives: identifying the individuals behind the drug trade and analysing weaknesses within the country’s enforcement mechanisms to prevent similar incidents. His explanation follows the seizure of 46.7 kilogrammes of cocaine at the Rafic Hariri International Airport in Beirut, Lebanon, in a consignment that originated from Accra. The seizure renewed concerns about Ghana’s involvement in international drug trafficking networks, particularly after questions emerged over NACOC’s decision to allow a suspected courier to travel to Lebanon with the consignment. The Commission has defended the decision, explaining that it formed part of a controlled-delivery operation intended to identify and apprehend other members of the international trafficking network. Three foreign nationals have subsequently been arrested in Ghana in connection with the shipment.

items.title: After midterm rout, Vance tries to build his own 2028 brand
items.description: Late in his blitz to salvage Republicans’ midterm fortunes, Vice President JD Vance shifted strategy. He talked less about President Donald Trump and more about the issues that define his own political identity. Vance argued the case for Republicans, who lost control of Congress in Tuesday’s vote , almost exclusively through the lens of his policy portfolio, according to a Reuters review of half a dozen speeches since the Republican convention in September. He bypassed Trump’s signature policies, including the Iran war and deportations , as polls showed the president’s sagging popularity dragging down Republican office-seekers. The change was deliberate, according to two people familiar with the strategy. Vance and his advisers saw the issues he championed — economic nationalism, foreign policy restraint and public safety as politically potent subjects he could address with authority. While Trump embraced them as part of his ‘Make America Great Again’ (MAGA) movement, Vance had emerged as their lead crusader, the people said. The shift offered an early glimpse of how the 42-year-old vice president could chart his own course as Republicans begin looking beyond Trump. Vance hasn’t said whether he will run for president in 2028, and Trump hasn’t endorsed him or anyone else. But Vance is viewed as a leading potential contender who some Republican officials say will need to inherit much of Trump’s coalition while separating himself from his boss’s baggage. Vance took a more public step on Wednesday toward reinforcing his own political brand with an unusually blunt election postmortem. In a social media post, he blamed the Iran war for Republicans’ midterm defeat and laid out a platform for a Republican rebound. He called for a swift end to the conflict and urged Republicans to focus on affordability, reevaluate foreign relations and overhaul the US relationship with Israel. Trump has called Americans’ affordability concerns a Democratic hoax. He launched a war against Iran following sustained lobbying from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Trump went on to endorse Netanyahu in the Israeli election. Vance makes unease at the war public The post, for the first time, put Vance openly on the side of ending the war. Three people familiar with the White House and Vance’s communications told Reuters that the vice president was not breaking with Trump and said White House chief of staff Susie Wiles knew in advance about Vance’s post. On Friday, Trump reshuffled senior White House leadership, replacing Wiles with Stephen Miller in a move that suggests the White House plans to double down on some of Trump’s more hardline policies. Trump has acknowledged the Iran war played a role in the Republican rout because of the resulting high gas prices but has continued to defend it. “I would have done nothing different,” he told reporters on Wednesday. A plume of smoke rises after a US-Israeli strike as loud explosions were heard in the central and eastern parts of the Iranian capital, Tehran on March 3, 2026. — AFP/File Reuters could not determine whether Trump was aware of the post in advance. Donald Trump Jr, the president’s eldest son, endorsed Vance’s remarks on social media, along with some conservative allies. The dialogue further elevated Vance as a potential post-Trump conservative standard-bearer, said Michael Ricci, a Republican strategist and former adviser to House Speakers John Boehner and Paul Ryan. Using the megaphone of the vice presidency He said Vance’s message forced conservatives to debate the merits of the war, and more broadly, what core tenets Republican presidential candidates should embrace in 2028. “It’s simplistic to say this about him looking for ways to differentiate himself from Trump,” Ricci said. “This is about him using his megaphone of the vice presidency to set the terms of debate.” Representatives for Vance declined to comment. White House representatives referred Reuters to Trump’s comments on Wednesday, when he told reporters he understood Vance’s perspective on the election results. US Vice President JD Vance arrives to speak at a midterm campaign rally on October 28, 2026 in Kinston, North Carolina, the US. — Reuters Democrats are poised to tie Vance or any Republican nominee to Trump in 2028, especially if Trump plays a large role in vetting conservative hopefuls. “There’s a real challenge of how you position yourself to be viable in a general election while winning a primary that still requires you to bow down and kiss the ring, said Igor Volsky, a Democratic strategist. Vance’s brand did not emerge from the midterms unscathed. Republicans lost in states where he campaigned. Some of the strategies he endorsed, including an ad by Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy that cast doubt on the sexual abuse suffered by the victorious Democratic candidate, Amy Acton, may have swung races away from Republicans. Other possible 2028 presidential contenders have offered their diagnoses of the midterm defeat. Texas Senator Ted Cruz said Republicans hadn’t done enough on affordability. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said losing candidates had focused too heavily on transgender issues and neglected voter concerns about data centres and artificial intelligence. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has stayed silent. Vance’s effort to shape the debate was visible during the closing days of the campaign. In stump speeches, he told voters to support Republicans because they would investigate fraud in federal health care and antipoverty programs, tying that to the White House’s immigration agenda and cost of living. He almost entirely ignored the Iran war and gas prices, and seldom mentioned Trump by name. “I want my kids to raise a family in a country that is vibrant and thriving and free and prosperous. I want the simple things,” Vance said at one of his final rallies in North Carolina. “And because I want that for me, I want it for you too.”

items.title: Retour des orpailleurs expulsés de Guinée : Une première vague de 3 400 Burkinabè accueillie à Bobo
items.description: Après leur expulsion de la Guinée et leur transit par le Mali, 3 400 Burkinabè ont foulé le sol national dans la nuit du 6 au 7 novembre 2026. Accueillis par une délégation gouvernementale au stade omnisports de Bobo-Dioulasso, ces compatriotes bénéficieront d'un accompagnement sanitaire, psychosocial et de mesures de réinsertion socioprofessionnelle.. Ce sont au total 48 cars transportant 3400 personnes qui sont arrivés à Bobo Dioulasso en provenance du Mali avec cette première vague.Ces jeunes ont été contraints de quitter la Guinée suite à la décision des autorités de ce pays de suspendre l'exploitation artisanale de l'or. « Nous rendons grâce à Dieu, ces 3400 personnes sont rentrées à bon port », se réjouit le ministre de la Famille et de la Solidarité, le lieutenant-colonel Passowindé Pélagie Kaboré/Kabre. Les membres du gouvernement ont remonté le moral à ces jeunes et les a rassurés : tout sera mis en place pour leur prise en charge et c'est ce qui justifie cette mobilisation du gouvernement pour les accueillir. « Nous sommes venus sur instructions du président du Faso, assister à l'arrivée du premier convoi revenu de Bamako avec nos compatriotes », a indiqué la ministre. Sur place, ils ont été vite pris en charge grâce à un dispositif d'accueil mis en place par le Conseil régional de secours d'urgence et de réhabilitation. Cet accueil consiste d'abord, à faire un check sécuritaire , ensuite un check sanitaire qui permet de prendre en charge les cas de maladies et de blessés et enfin une prise en charge psycho-sociale. « Au niveau de la zone de prise en charge psychosociale , il y aura le profilage et bien-sûr, on va essayer de leur trouver de petites commodités pour leur permettre de se reposer avant de pouvoir continuer…Les mineurs seront retenus mais les jeunes adultes vont être enregistrés et chacun pourra rejoindre sa famille », a précisé le ministre. Et ce n'est pas tout. Le gouvernement propose des solutions de relèvement à travers le retour des enfants mineurs à l'école , la réinsertion socioprofessionnelle pour ceux qui vont opter pour la formation professionnelle. Il compte également ouvrir les portes des universités aux jeunes titulaires du BAC, pour leur permettre de poursuivre leur cursus universitaire, a expliqué le ministre chargé de la solidarité. Lefaso.net Source : Page facebook du ministère en charge de l'Enseignement supérieur

items.title: La Tunisie embourbée dans le problème des migrants irréguliers
items.description: La Tunisie officielle rejette l’idée de faire du pays un territoire d’accueil permanent pour les migrants en situation irrégulière en route vers l’Europe. Sauf qu’en réalité, la Tunisie est en passe de devenir un territoire de transit ou d’installation pour beaucoup de migrants irréguliers, notamment subsahariens, généralement entrés par les frontières algériennes et libyennes. Ce qui pose des problèmes sécuritaires et sociaux et alimente la colère d’un bon nombre de Tunisiens, notamment les plus démunis, qui pensent, non sans raison, que la présence de ces personnes – dont les autorités évitent d’estimer le nombre réel – aggrave la situation économique et sociale dans un pays déjà en crise. (Photo : Pour quelques milliers de migrants irréguliers retournés chez eux, combien entrent chaque jour au pays et combien dépensent l'argent que leur donne l'OIM et reviennent par les mêmes voies?) Imed Bahri La Tunisie continuera à lutter contre les réseaux criminels impliqués dans le trafic de migrants et la traite des êtres humains, a déclaré le ministre des Affaires étrangères, de la Migration et des Tunisiens à l’étranger, Mohamed Ali Nafti, lors d’une réunion conjointe des commissions parlementaires de l’Assemblée des représentants du peuple (ARP) et du Conseil national des régions et des districts (CNRD), vendredi 6 novembre 2026, consacrée à l’examen du budget de son ministère pour 2027, réaffirmant au passage le refus du pays de devenir un pays de transit ou d’installation pour les migrants en situation irrégulière, ou encore une plateforme de débarquement pour les migrants et les demandeurs d’asile. Le chef de la diplomatie tunisienne a réaffirmé la détermination du gouvernement à défendre la souveraineté nationale, à protéger les frontières et à combattre les organisations criminelles qui exploitent les flux migratoires. Il a toutefois souligné que la politique migratoire tunisienne repose sur une approche globale intégrant les dimensions humanitaires, économiques, sociales et de développement, dans le respect de la dignité et des droits des migrants. Selon les données communiquées par les autorités tunisiennes lors d'une rencontre entre M. Nafti et la directrice générale de l’OIM, Amy Pope, à New York le 22 septembre dernier, 5 077 retours volontaires avaient été enregistrés depuis le début de l’année 2026 dans le cadre du mécanisme d’assistance et de réintégration. Cela porte à 25 351 le nombre total de bénéficiaires du programme, sans compter les retours effectués via des vols commerciaux réguliers. Migrants subsahariens l Ce que la Tunisie refuse de voir Pour quelques départs, combien d'entrées ? La position exprimée par le ministre s’inscrit dans la ligne politique du président Kaïs Saïed, qui rejette l’idée de faire de la Tunisie un territoire d’accueil permanent pour les migrants en situation irrégulière en route vers l’Europe. Sauf que la lutte contre la migration irrégulière en empêchant les migrants de rejoindre les côtes européennes, si elle baisse les flux de leurs arrivées sur les côtes italiennes, elle ne sert pas les intérêts de la Tunisie, qui se trouve submergée, du nord au sud, de l'est à l'ouest, dans pratiquement toutes les villes côtières, par une population qu’elle n’a pas les moyens de nourrir, d’abriter, d’éduquer et de soigner… Ne nous voilons pas la face : pour quelques milliers de migrants irréguliers retournés chez eux, combien entrent chaque jour au pays et combien dépensent l'argent du retour que leur donne l'OIM et reviennent à notre pays par les mêmes voies? En d'autres termes, les gesticulations ne règlent pas les problèmes; elles servent parfois à cacher la réalité qu'elles dénoncent. N'est-ce pas M. Nafti ? L’article La Tunisie embourbée dans le problème des migrants irréguliers est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Guinée : l'opposant Aliou Bah libéré après une grâce présidentielle
items.description: Le president du Mouvement democratique liberal (MoDeL) a recouvre la liberte le 6 novembre, a annonce sa formation politique dans un communique publie a Conakry. Âge de 42 ans, il avait ete arrete le 26 decembre 2024, alors qu'il s'appretait a se rendre en Sierra Leone. Cette liberation intervient apres une grâce presidentielle accordee le 2 octobre par le general Mamadi Doumbouya, a l'occasion de la celebration du 67e anniversaire de l'independance de la Guinee. La mesure etait toutefois assortie d'un stage d'encadrement civique et de preparation a la reinsertion d'une duree de 45 jours, que l'opposant devait effectuer avant de retrouver sa liberte. En janvier 2025, Aliou Bah avait ete condamne a deux ans de prison ferme pour « offense et diffamation envers le chef de l'etat ». Il avait toujours conteste les accusations portees contre lui. Dans son communique, le MoDeL exprime son soulagement apres la liberation de son president et remercie les avocats, les militants, les sympathisants ainsi que les organisations nationales et internationales de defense des droits humains qui lui ont apporte leur soutien durant sa detention. Le parti salue egalement la mobilisation de la societe civile, des responsables politiques et des medias ayant suivi cette affaire. Au-dela de la liberation de son dirigeant, le MoDeL entend maintenir son positionnement politique. La formation reaffirme son engagement en faveur des principes democratiques, du respect des libertes fondamentales et de la primaute du droit.

items.title: Explainer: What INEC’s 2023 results in Lagos, Oyo, Osun actually reveal
items.description: By Omeiza Ajayi, ABUJA Lagos, Oyo and Osun states each backed a different candidate in the February 25, 2023 presidential election, according to the results declared by the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC. Read Also: How Buhari promised me APC presidential ticket in 2022; I regret listening to him – Amaechi Peter Obi of the Labour Party, LP, won Lagos; Bola Tinubu of the All Progressives Congress, APC, won Oyo, and Atiku Abubakar of the Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, won Osun. What happened in Lagos? Lagos produced the closest of the three contests. Obi polled 582,454 votes (45.81 per cent), while Tinubu, the APC candidate, followed with 572,606 votes (45.04 per cent). The gap was 9,848 votes, less than one percentage point. Atiku trailed far behind with 75,750 votes (5.96 per cent), and Rabiu Kwankwaso of the New Nigeria Peoples Party, NNPP, had 8,442 votes (0.66 per cent). What happened in Oyo? Oyo was not close. Tinubu polled 449,884 votes (55.58 per cent), well ahead of Atiku’s 182,977 votes (22.60 per cent). His lead of 266,907 votes was the widest of the three states. Obi came third in Oyo with 99,110 votes (12.24 per cent), and Kwankwaso had 4,095 votes (0.51 per cent). What happened in Osun? Osun was nearly as tight as Lagos. Atiku won with 354,366 votes (46.88 per cent), while Tinubu had 343,945 votes (45.50 per cent), a difference of 10,421 votes. Obi finished third with 23,283 votes, and Kwankwaso had 713 votes (0.09 per cent). What the combined figures show Added together, the results tell a story that the three winners alone do not. Tinubu won only one of the states, yet he finished first or second in all three and polled 1,366,435 votes across them. Obi, who topped the Lagos poll, totalled 704,847 votes across the three states because he fell to third in both Oyo and Osun. Atiku polled 613,093 votes, and Kwankwaso finished fourth in each state, with 13,250 votes combined. Put differently, Obi’s win came by the thinnest of margins in the most populous of the three states. But Tinubu’s lead in Oyo was large enough to leave him comfortably ahead of both rivals on the combined tally. Vanguard News The post Explainer: What INEC’s 2023 results in Lagos, Oyo, Osun actually reveal appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Pakistan, Sudan sign visa-free travel agreement for official, diplomatic passport holders
items.description: Pakistan and Sudan on Saturday signed an agreement on visa-free travel for official and diplomatic passport holders, according to a statement by the Ministry of Interior. “Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi and Sudanese Interior Minister Lt Gen Babiker Samra Mustafa Ali signed the agreement,” the ministry said on the social media platform X. “Under the agreement, holders of Pakistani and Sudanese official and diplomatic passports will be able to enter each other’s countries without a visa,” it stated. “Both interior ministers welcomed the visa-free entry agreement for official and diplomatic passports,” the statement said. “This agreement marks an important milestone in bilateral relations between Pakistan and Sudan,” it added. The statement emphasised that the visa-free facility would further facilitate high-level contacts and exchanges of delegations between Pakistan and Sudan. “New opportunities will emerge to promote official-level ties and mutual cooperation between the two countries.” “The agreement will further strengthen friendly relations and institutional cooperation between Pakistan and Sudan, the Sudanese interior minister was quoted as saying. “Both interior ministers reaffirmed their commitment to further consolidating and strengthening bilateral relations,” the statement added. Earlier on Saturday, both countries also decided to sign a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to enhance cooperation in combating cybercrime, the statement by the interior ministry said. The decision was taken during delegation-level talks between interior ministers of both countries. Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry also attended the meeting. The Sudanese interior minister said his country wanted to benefit from Pakistan’s expertise and experience in combating cybercrime, the statement said. “The two sides also agreed to expand cooperation in security, internal affairs, police training, institutional cooperation, the National Database and Registration Authority (Nadra) and other sectors.” “Pakistan is ready to extend all possible cooperation to Sudan in peace-building and reconstruction,” Naqvi was quoted as saying. “Pakistan is also ready to provide professional training to Sudanese police officers,” the interior minister said during the meeting. Briefing the visiting minister, Naqvi said that with Nadra’s cooperation, 36 million citizenship cards, 9 million national identity cards, 18 million birth certificates and 500,000 death certificates had been issued in Sudan. He said Nadra was ready to continue cooperation in the civil registration process. On a query by the Sudanese minister, Naqvi ordered immediate resolution of visa issues faced by married Sudanese women in Pakistan, the statement said. “Sudanese citizens can avail medical facilities in Pakistan and will be provided every possible facility in the health sector,” Naqvi said. “Pakistan is a brotherly country and Sudan attaches great importance to cooperation with it in all fields,” the Sudanese interior minister was quoted as saying. He expressed the desire to promote cooperation in various sectors and thanked Pakistan for its cooperation. A day ago, the Sudanese interior minister held a meeting with Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and discussed avenues to enhance bilateral cooperation between their countries. On Thursday, he also met Prime Minister Shahbaz Sharif. In a meeting with the prime minister, he commended Pakistan’s support on international forums regarding efforts to restore peace and security in Sudan.

items.title: Marche Verte : 51 ans après, la diplomatie royale à l’heure de la consécration
items.description: À l’occasion du 51e anniversaire de la Marche Verte, les récents développements autour du dossier du Sahara replacent la diplomatie marocaine au centre de l’actualité internationale. Entre évolution des rapports de force au Conseil de sécurité, soutien de plusieurs puissances et progression de l’initiative d’autonomie, cette séquence est présentée comme le prolongement, sur le terrain diplomatique, de la mobilisation historique du 6 novembre 1975. Pour le chercheur en sciences politiques; Mohamed Chahbi, la séquence diplomatique d’octobre 2026 marque une nouvelle étape dans le dossier du Sahara. Dans une analyse consacrée à cette commémoration, il met en avant le rôle de la diplomatie royale, le positionnement des grandes puissances et la progression du soutien international à l’initiative marocaine d’autonomie. La Marche Verte a changé de terrain sans perdre sa portée historique, estime-t-il, notant qu'après avoir mobilisé des centaines de milliers de Marocains en novembre 1975, elle se poursuit désormais dans les enceintes diplomatiques internationales et les grandes capitales. Le chercheur considère ainsi que les développements enregistrés au Conseil de sécurité des Nations unies à la fin du mois d’octobre constituent une nouvelle illustration de cette continuité. Il qualifie la séquence diplomatique récente de « chef-d’œuvre de realpolitik » , relevant que le Maroc a réussi à faire évoluer le rapport de force autour du dossier du Sahara grâce à une stratégie conduite sur la durée. La vision royale au cœur de la stratégie diplomatique Dans son analyse, Mohamed Chahbi attribue cette évolution à la vision stratégique du Roi Mohammed VI et à la conduite de la diplomatie marocaine. Il met particulièrement en avant le rôle du Cabinet royal, qu’il présente comme un acteur central dans la coordination de cette orientation. « Ce triomphe du réalisme n’est pas le fruit du hasard. Il est le couronnement d’une vision stratégique inébranlable, orchestrée avec une efficience rare. Sous l'impulsion de Souverain, la diplomatie marocaine a fait preuve d'une maturité exceptionnelle, tissant une toile de fond où l’Initiative d’Autonomie s'est imposée non plus comme une simple proposition, mais comme l'unique horizon crédible, le socle exclusif de tout avenir pour la région », éctit-il. Le chercheur estime que l’initiative marocaine d’autonomie a progressivement acquis une place prépondérante dans les discussions internationales. À ses yeux, elle ne constitue plus simplement une proposition parmi d’autres, mais s’est imposée comme « l’unique horizon crédible » pour parvenir à une solution au différend régional. Rabat, poursuit-il, aborde désormais ce dossier avec une position consolidée, sans attendre que les Nations unies élaborent une nouvelle formule. Dans cette lecture, l’objectif consiste à inscrire les évolutions diplomatiques dans un cadre international prenant en compte les réalités établies sur le terrain. Des rapports de force internationaux en évolution Mohamed Chahbi voit dans les positionnements enregistrés au cours du mois d’octobre 2026, le signe d'un recul des thèses opposées à la position marocaine. Il cite notamment le changement d’orientation de la Colombie, intervenu en août dernier, qu’il considère comme un tournant susceptible de renforcer la position du Maroc en Amérique latine. Le chercheur estime que cette évolution, conjuguée aux dynamiques diplomatiques observées dans d’autres régions du monde, témoigne d’une progression de l’approche marocaine. Il évoque également les positions exprimées au Conseil de sécurité, notamment les abstentions de la Russie, de la Chine et du Pakistan, qu’il interprète comme le signe de l’absence d’une alternative bénéficiant d’un consensus international. À ce sujet, il considère que ces abstentions ne doivent pas être interprétées comme un revers pour Rabat, mais plutôt une illustration des limites rencontrées par les positions concurrentes face à la dynamique diplomatique marocaine. Le chercheur se montre par ailleurs particulièrement critique à l’égard de l’option référendaire, qu’il juge dépassée et désormais inadaptée à l’évolution du dossier. « Face à ce raz-de-marée de pragmatisme, les adversaires de l'intégrité territoriale du Maroc se heurtent à un mur. Leurs tentatives de brouillage, qu'elles soient militaires dans les zones tampons ou médiatiques, se fracassent contre la solidité du droit international. L'option référendaire, obsolète et enterrée par l'Histoire, n'est plus qu'un mirage pour les seuls aveugles », souligne-t-il. Un soutien qui s’étend à plusieurs régions du monde Mohamed Chahbi souligne également le poids des soutiens exprimés par plusieurs puissances occidentales. Il cite notamment les États-Unis, dont le soutien s’inscrit, selon lui, dans la continuité de leur reconnaissance de la souveraineté marocaine sur le Sahara, ainsi que la France et le Royaume-Uni. Il accorde une place particulière à l’évolution des positions en Afrique et dans le monde arabe. L’ouverture de consulats à Laâyoune et à Dakhla par plusieurs pays, dont la République démocratique du Congo, le Liberia et Bahreïn, est présentée comme un indicateur concret de l’ancrage de ces relations. Il mentionne également le soutien de la Somalie et le vote du Panama parmi les développements qu’il juge significatifs. « C'est sur le continent africain et dans le monde arabe que le génie diplomatique marocain rayonne le plus. L'ouverture des consulats à Dakhla et Laâyoune par des pays frères comme la RDC, le Liberia ou Bahreïn, tout comme le soutien de la Somalie ou le vote historique du Panama, prouve que le Maroc n'est plus seulement une puissance régionale, mais un acteur global incontournable », fait-il observer à ce propos. Pour le chercheur, cette dynamique confirme que le Maroc a renforcé son statut d’acteur diplomatique de premier plan, dont l’influence dépasse désormais son environnement régional immédiat. La Marche Verte, une dynamique qui se poursuit Revenant sur la portée de la commémoration du 6 novembre, Mohamed Chahbi estime que la diplomatie marocaine a pris le relais de la mobilisation populaire de 1975. Il considère que les acquis diplomatiques enregistrés ces dernières années prolongent l’élan de la Marche Verte et traduisent la continuité d’une stratégie portée au plus haut niveau de l’État. Dans cette perspective, le Sahara constitue, selon lui, un levier du rayonnement du Maroc sur les plans continental et international. Le chercheur conclut que la Marche Verte ne saurait être réduite à un épisode historique, mais représente une dynamique appelée à se poursuivre : « Elle est une énergie perpétuelle. Et aujourd'hui, plus d'un demi-siècle après, elle continue de résonner, victorieuse et éternelle, des dunes de Laâyoune jusqu'aux travées de New York ». items.title: What Happened to JetBlue?
items.description: For airlines in the United States, going bankrupt is practically a rite of passage. Since the airline industry was deregulated almost 50 years ago, dozens of airlines have filed for Chapter 11, including each of the so-called Big Three carriers—United, American, and Delta. A notable exception has been JetBlue, which until recently was one of the industry’s few success stories. But after The Wall Street Journal reported last month that the airline’s mounting debt obligations moved senior creditors to hire restructuring advisers, some investors began assuming that bankruptcy was on the way. JetBlue’s CEO, Joanna Geraghty, insists otherwise. On the company’s most recent earnings call, in late October, she at least temporarily assuaged investor anxieties with claims that the airline was not at risk of going under, and was on track to return to profitability next year. Even so, JetBlue is undoubtedly struggling. The carrier has lost more than $3 billion since 2019, the last year it turned a full-year profit, and its debt load has risen swiftly to about $8.4 billion. The proximate cause of the company’s current woes is obvious: Fuel costs have soared since the Iran war began. But the challenge the company faces is more fundamental than that. JetBlue has been struggling because it finds itself in what’s sometimes called the “mushy middle,” caught between discount airlines on the low end and the big legacy carriers, which have lots of expense-account-wielding business travelers and lucrative transatlantic routes, on the high end. [ Read: An SNL sketch to make airlines feel ashamed ] When JetBlue began flying, in 2000, being in between was a strength: The company explicitly positioned itself as a stylish and plucky alternative to the ultra-low-cost carriers and the legacy carriers. It offered more legroom, good snacks, free satellite television, and leather seats to every customer, but still managed to be significantly cheaper than the big airlines. It was able to pull this off because its jet fleet was made up of only one type of plane, which kept maintenance costs down, and its workforce was not unionized. The carrier also initially offered just one class of seat, which helped it maximize space, even with the extra legroom.JetBlue’s marketing leaned into the idea that the company offered a new model for the industry, promising to “bring humanity back to air travel.” The carrier was so successful so quickly that legacy airlines tried to adopt this model for themselves: Delta and United started lower-cost, would-be JetBlue competitors in the 2000s, but both quickly failed. Meanwhile, JetBlue expanded its relatively low-cost, high-value offerings; in 2014, it launched a premium cabin for transcontinental routes called Mint, featuring lie-flat seats and fares well below those of the big carriers. By the late 2010s, it was the fifth-biggest airline in the country. Over much of the past decade, though, that sweet spot in the market that JetBlue had made its own has shrunk. On the low end, new discount airlines have sprung up, offering no frills but also very cheap fares. On the higher end, the legacy carriers have gotten better at exploiting their lucrative revenue sources, jacking up prices on business travel and transatlantic routes, and using their giant customer bases to partner with credit-card companies willing to pay them billions. JetBlue has found it hard to keep up. Even if the carrier had wanted to slash prices to compete with the discounters, its costs are now far too high for it to do so. Those jets that were brand-new when the company launched are aging, driving up maintenance costs, and its workforce began unionizing in 2014, driving up labor costs. (It also does not want to give up on the premium amenities that have made it so distinctive.) At the same time, JetBlue has struggled to compete with the legacy carriers for more profitable business travelers because most of its planes lack business- or first-class cabins, and the company doesn’t fly to nearly as many cities as the legacy carriers do. Nor has it been able to leverage its loyalty program, TrueBlue, the way the big carriers have leveraged theirs. TrueBlue will generate about $1 billion in revenue for the airline this year, which seems impressive until you realize that Delta makes more than $8 billion annually from the SkyMiles credit cards issued by American Express. [ Read: The only thing worse than Spirit Airlines ] These problems are in some respects specific to the airline industry. But JetBlue’s troubles are also emblematic of a basic fact about American business, which is that it has simply become harder for companies targeting the middle of the market to succeed. Traditional department stores such as Macy’s and Kohl’s have found themselves squeezed between big-box retailers and e-tailers such as Walmart, Target, and Amazon on the low end and premium retailers on the high end. Casual sit-down restaurants including Applebee’s and TGI Fridays have gotten edged out by fast-casual restaurants and fine dining. The disappearance of the American-made passenger car is also part of this story: Cars such as the Chrysler Sebring and the Chevy Malibu weren’t cheap enough, relative to their perceived level of quality, to compete with the perennially reliable Toyota Camry and Honda Accord, but they also weren’t fancy enough to compete with Lexus and Tesla. Consumers have become more price-conscious and are better informed about quality and cachet. So offering a pretty-good option at an almost-premium price doesn’t cut it anymore. JetBlue is not doomed. It still has valuable assets, including most notably its brand, which remains surprisingly strong—even if it’s now doing many of the things that annoy people about traditional airlines, such as raising baggage fees. Its planes still have more legroom and free Wi-Fi. And next month, the carrier is going to be rolling out first-class cabins on many of its domestic routes, which should boost revenue. When fuel costs come down, the company may well turn a profit again. But being JetBlue is never going to be easy. It’s stuck in the middle, and these days, that’s the toughest place for a business to be.

items.title: ICE After the Blowout
items.description: “D eportations will continue,” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin wrote in a post on X the day after voters punished his party in the midterm election. The three-word statement appeared to be aimed at quieting an incipient debate among Republicans over whether President Trump should ease his ICE crackdown. Two years after he won back the White House promising the largest mass-deportation campaign in U.S. history, Trump and his party suffered monumental losses in states such as Texas, Georgia, and North Carolina, where voters—especially Hispanics—swung hard to Democrats. More moderate Republicans have urged the administration to adopt a quieter enforcement approach, focusing more narrowly on criminal offenders. Although the president has reportedly expressed concern to those close to him that some ICE tactics have gone too far, he has not ordered specific policy changes, according to three senior officials I spoke with at DHS. Those officials and others I’ve talked to told me they aren’t expecting a pullback, either. Trump’s decision to name Stephen Miller as his chief of staff yesterday places the chief architect and principal ideologue of the ICE campaign in charge of his administration. Miller’s promotion will give him even more power to mobilize other federal agencies to help ICE maximize deportations. Since Trump’s return to the White House, Republicans in Congress have given the administration nearly a quarter of a trillion dollars for the crackdown, aiming for 1 million deportations a year. ICE has obtained upwards of $110 billion, more than 11 times its annual budget, and the funding surge has created a powerful inertia. Absent a major policy reversal from Trump or a successful intervention by Democratic majorities in Congress—a longshot, experts say—Trump’s mass-deportation campaign will continue with its mandate to add more officers, more deportation flights, and more immigration jails. The campaign includes handing out wads of cash to local police and sheriff departments, which help the agency boost arrests. Prior to the midterms, ICE launched a hiring push to add 5,000 more employees—mosty deportation officers—by the end of the year. “Regardless of the political pressures that the White House may be feeling on immigration enforcement, the money creates a huge amount of momentum on its own,” Sarah Pierce, an immigration policy expert at the center-left think tank Third Way, told me. ICE has so much money that it will have to double its rate of spending to use it all before its deadline at the end of the 2029 fiscal year, she said. “Pulling that back would be extremely difficult for the White House.” [ Read: Losing the ‘big-ass truck’ vote ] Despite the midterm results, there hasn’t been a broad consensus in the Republican Party that overzealous ICE tactics were a vulnerability, and some right-wing commentators have pointed to exit-poll data showing that immigration was the top motivating issue for Republican voter turnout. At a polling place in the Dallas suburbs where I spoke with voters on Tuesday, several of the Republican supporters I met said they wanted Trump to stay the course. “Gotta keep locking it down,” said Danny, a 32-year-old hospital staffer I met outside a public library in Plano, north of Dallas. Danny told me he didn’t want his last name published, because he worried that he’d be harassed. His hometown and surrounding Collin County were reliably Republican when he was growing up, he said, but the region’s economic boom had brought in more transplants. “They keep voting for Democrats,” he said. “Democrats vote for more immigration. It’s a vicious cycle.” James Talarico, the Democratic winner of the Senate race in Texas, won Collin County by 12 points on Tuesday, a 23-point swing from Trump’s 2024 victory. It was the first time this century that Democrats have won statewide races in the county. Trump won nearly half the Hispanic vote nationwide in 2024, but this year Hispanics are estimated to have voted for Democrats by a 69–29 percent margin. C ould Democrats use their large majorities in Congress next year to force the administration to rein in ICE? Claire Trickler-McNulty, an attorney who has held several high-ranking roles at ICE, most recently during the Biden administration, told me that it will be hard for Democrats to change the trajectory of ICE spending. If Democrats pass an appropriations bill with language constraining or shifting ICE funds, Trump would have to sign it. “I don’t have a lot of confidence that he would sign that, but people I’ve talked to on the Hill feel like there may be a window or a path to a clawback, if you combine that with something he cares about,” Trickler-McNulty said. Trump has said he doesn’t want to spend the next two years “vetoing everything,” although the White House has also circulated a photo of a red VETO hat sitting on the Resolute Desk with the president in the background. Trump told Politico late Tuesday night that he’d be willing to work with Democrats on immigration reform if it were “appropriate and good for the country.” But the possibility of such negotiations could reduce the likelihood that Trump orders a different tack for ICE in the meantime. Mark Krikorian, the executive director of the Center for Immigration Studies, a leading immigration-restrictionist group, told me that the Trump administration has already shifted tactics, and could do so again. After the killings of two U.S. citizens in Minneapolis in January, Trump demoted Greg Bovino , the performative Border Patrol commander who was leading the crackdown in the city, and replaced Kristi Noem with Mullin, who said he wanted a more low-key ICE approach. That change marked the end of what Krikorian described as “theatricality,” generating ready-for-TV images of masked federal forces staging operations that thrilled the president’s base. But Krikorian said that an “imbalance” remains between “body-armor enforcement versus briefcase enforcement.” Trump could direct ICE to conduct more enforcement at worksites—not necessarily with raids that would send people running, Krikorian said, but with mundane audits that check Social Security numbers and other documents. “Worksite enforcement is something that has been very much lacking in this administration,” he said. It’s a lot less photogenic and a lot less politically tumultuous to just send in some bureaucrats.” [ Read: The secretary of homeland ] ICE continued to ramp up, with less fanfare, after Minneapolis , and the agency is now making more than 50,000 arrests a month, its highest rate ever. Officers have achieved those levels in part by using automated technologies, such as license-plate readers, and powerful database tools to make more traffic stops. Those public encounters deepened the backlash to ICE over the summer when officers shot several unarmed immigrants—two fatally—as they attempted to drive away. City and state governments have joined in that backlash, a trend that could accelerate with the widespread Democratic victories this week. The mayor of Houston announced yesterday that the city’s police will no longer contact ICE about nonviolent offenders who lack legal status. White-collar enforcement would not necessarily lead to arrests and deportations, but it would make it more likely for immigrants who are in the United States illegally to leave on their own, Krikorian said. The frustrations that Trump has been hearing from business owners may weigh against a crackdown on employers. Vice President Vance, who is considering running for president in 2028, appeared to signal a preference for that approach on Wednesday in a lengthy X post that assessed the party’s defeat. Vance wrote that he was “open” to shifting ICE’s focus to businesses that “hire illegal labor,” but said he didn’t support “amnesty,” the catch-all term used by immigration hard-liners who oppose creating a path to legal status for the estimated 12 million to 15 million immigrants who are illegally present in the United States. “Anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you,” Vance wrote. Pierce told me that she interpreted Vance’s post as a defense of the administration’s crackdown that was aimed at Republicans who view the midterm results as a rebuke. She said she’ll be watching to see if pressure on the administration to change tactics builds in the coming weeks or if the White House remains defensive and determined to follow the same course. [ Read: Repudiation ] There were also signs in Vance’s post of the conundrum that he and other potential Republican presidential candidates will likely face if they try to succeed Trump. Although there is broad support across the electorate for the deportation of immigrants who commit violent crimes or pose a threat to public safety, those immigrants represent only 10 to 20 percent of ICE arrests. Trump officials have spent the past two years appealing to the most ardent members of the MAGA movement, especially those who want DHS to be a tool of social and demographic transformation through the removal and “remigration” of millions of immigrants. Those views are too extreme for most voters in a general presidential election. But to win the party’s primaries, Vance, or any other potential Republican candidate, may need to embrace them. Ashley Parker and Michael Scherer contributed reporting.
